method: Each claim checked against the retrieved text of the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Febrile seizure' (last updated February 2026, PIC endorsed), including key points, background, genetics, history, examination, the simple/complex classification table, investigations, treatment, consultation, transfer, discharge, outpatient follow-up, parent information links and both reference lists. Lumbar puncture is not mentioned anywhere in the retrieved text and no position on it is asserted. Antipyretic and fever management are deferred by the source to a separate Febrile child guideline and are marked out_of_scope. UpToDate and BMJ Best Practice are cited by the source and are subscription content, cited by reference only and not reproduced. Two artefacts are disclosed: the temperature threshold renders as '380C' for 38 degrees Celsius, transcribed verbatim in source_text and rendered as the evident value in the guideline; and the page carries two versions of its own reference list, one viewed 26 September 2025 and one viewed May 2019.

claims.claim: The guideline's key points are that most febrile seizures are benign and do not require further investigation, that management includes identifying and managing the source of infection, and that antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions
claims.source_text:
1. Most febrile seizures are benign and do not require further investigation
2. Management includes identifying and managing the source of infection
3. Antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions

claims.claim: A febrile seizure is defined as a seizure associated with a fever of at least 38 degrees Celsius in a young child without central nervous system infection, electrolyte imbalance, or a history of afebrile seizures
claims.source_text:
Definition: a seizure associated with a fever (of at least 380C) in a young child without any of the following:
    - central nervous system infection
    - electrolyte imbalance
    - a history of afebrile seizures

claims.claim: Febrile seizures usually occur between 6 months and 6 years of age and are normally associated with simple viral infections
claims.source_text:
Usually occur between 6 months and 6 years of age
  - Normally associated with simple viral infections

claims.claim: Younger children are more likely to have a further febrile seizure, with a 50 per cent risk of recurrence in a 1-year-old child and a 30 per cent risk of recurrence in a 2-year-old child
claims.source_text:
Younger children are more likely to have a further febrile seizure
    - 50% risk of recurrence in 1-year-old child
    - 30% risk of recurrence in 2-year-old child

claims.claim: The background prevalence risk of febrile seizures is 1 in 30, rising to 1 in 5 where one sibling is affected and to 1 in 3 if both parents and a previous child have had previous febrile seizures
claims.source_text:
Background prevalence risk of 1 in 30
    - Rises to 1 in 5 where one sibling is affected
    - Rises to 1 in 3 if both parents and a previous child have had previous febrile seizures

claims.claim: No single susceptibility gene for febrile seizure is known, and genes have been identified in families with genetic epilepsies with febrile seizures plus spectrum known as GEFS plus
claims.source_text: No single susceptibility gene for febrile seizure is known … Genes have been identified in families with "genetic epilepsies with febrile seizures plus spectrum" (GEFS+)

claims.claim: Genetic testing may be recommended in specific higher-risk groups, for example prolonged febrile seizures in children less than 18 months
claims.source_text: Genetic testing may be recommended in specific higher-risk groups, eg prolonged febrile seizures in children less than 18 months

claims.claim: History should cover onset of illness, determining the source of the fever such as viral, gastroenteritis or UTI, and seizure characteristics including duration, generalised versus focal features, length of post ictal period and return to neurological baseline
claims.source_text:
Onset of illness
  - Determine source of the fever eg viral, gastroenteritis, UTI
  - Seizure characteristics
    - duration
    - generalised versus focal features
    - length of post ictal period
    - return to neurological baseline

claims.claim: History should screen for alternative causes of presentation such as seizure mimickers, cardiac dysrhythmia and underlying metabolic syndromes, and should cover history of neurological conditions, history of developmental delay or regression, and family history of febrile seizures, epilepsy or sudden cardiac death
claims.source_text:
Screen for alternative causes of presentation, eg seizure mimickers, cardiac dysrhythmia, underlying metabolic syndromes
  - History of neurological conditions
  - History of developmental delay or regression
  - Family history of febrile seizures, epilepsy or sudden cardiac death

claims.claim: Examination should identify the source of infection and include a neurological examination to confirm return to neurological baseline
claims.source_text:
Identify source of infection
  - Neurological examination
    - Confirm return to neurological baseline

claims.claim: Red flags suggestive of CNS infection are complex febrile seizure, meningism including bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness and photophobia, and prolonged postictal altered consciousness of more than 1 hour
claims.source_text:
Red flags suggestive of CNS infection
      - complex febrile seizure
      - meningism (bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, photophobia)
      - prolonged postictal altered consciousness (>1 Hour)

claims.claim: Examination should look for neurocutaneous stigmata such as facial port-wine stain, facial angiofibroma, hypopigmented macules and cafe au lait spots
claims.source_text: Neurocutaneous stigmata, eg facial port-wine stain, facial angiofibroma, hypopigmented macules, café au lait spots

claims.claim: A simple febrile seizure is generalised tonic-clonic and of duration less than 15 minutes and with complete recovery in less than 1 hour and does not recur within the same illness
claims.source_text:
| **Simple febrile seizure** | **Complex febrile seizure** | | --- | --- | | Generalised tonic-clonic, and
Duration <15 min, and
Complete recovery <1 hour, and
Does not recur within same illness

claims.claim: An afebrile febrile seizure is defined as meeting the simple febrile seizure criteria but occurring during an acute infectious illness without a documented fever
claims.source_text: **Afebrile febrile seizure:** as above but occurring during an acute infectious illness without a documented fever

claims.claim: A complex febrile seizure has focal features, or duration more than 15 minutes, or persistent altered mental status of more than 1 hour, or recurrence within the same illness
claims.source_text:
Focal features, or
Duration >15 min, or
Persistent altered mental status (>1 hour), or
Recurrence within same illness

claims.claim: A prolonged febrile seizure is a complex febrile seizure with duration more than 30 minutes and may be associated with genetic epilepsy syndromes
claims.source_text: **Prolonged febrile seizure:** as above with duration >30 minutes - may be associated with genetic epilepsy syndromes

claims.claim: A simple febrile seizure does not require additional investigations beyond any required for investigation of the fever, and additional blood tests and neuroimaging are low yield and risk exposing the child to unnecessary painful procedure and/or radiation
claims.source_text:
A simple febrile seizure does not require additional investigations beyond any required for investigation of the fever
    - Additional blood tests and neuroimaging are low yield and risk exposing the child to unnecessary painful procedure and/or radiation

claims.claim: Targeted investigations are recommended in atypical presentations or with complex febrile seizures, including blood glucose level and serum electrolytes to exclude a provoked seizure and an ECG to exclude a seizure mimicker
claims.source_text:
Targeted investigations are recommended in atypical presentations or with complex febrile seizures
    - Exclude provoked seizure: BGL, serum electrolytes
    - Exclude seizure mimicker: ECG

claims.claim: Investigations should be performed in children who appear seriously unwell, and red flags for serious infection include complex febrile seizures, persistent altered mental status of more than 1 hour, signs of sepsis, meningitis or encephalitis, and incomplete immunisation against Haemophilus influenzae B or Streptococcus pneumoniae
claims.source_text:
Investigations should be performed in children who appear seriously unwell … Red flags for serious infection include

    - Complex febrile seizures
    - Persistent altered mental status (>1 hour)
    - Signs of sepsis, meningitis or encephalitis
    - Incomplete immunisation against _Haemophilus influenzae B_ or _Streptococcus pneumoniae_

claims.claim: In a complex febrile seizure CNS imaging should be considered after consultation with a senior doctor
claims.source_text: In a complex febrile seizure, consider CNS imaging after consultation with a senior doctor

claims.claim: The seizure should be treated if duration is ongoing after 5 minutes, referring to the afebrile seizures guideline
claims.source_text: Treat the seizure if duration ongoing after **5 minutes**, see

claims.claim: Management includes managing the underlying cause of the fever, and children with simple febrile seizures have the equivalent risk of serious bacterial infection as those with fever alone
claims.source_text:
Manage the underlying cause of the fever
    - Children with simple febrile seizures have the equivalent risk of serious bacterial infection as those with fever alone

claims.claim: Ongoing treatment with antiepileptic drugs is not routinely recommended
claims.source_text: Ongoing treatment with antiepileptic drugs is not routinely recommended

claims.claim: Consultation with the local paediatric team should be considered for a complex febrile seizure or concern for serious bacterial infection as cause of febrile seizure
claims.source_text:
Complex febrile seizure
  - Concern for serious bacterial infection as cause of febrile seizure

claims.claim: Transfer should be considered for respiratory or haemodynamic compromise, prolonged febrile seizure, persistent altered mental status of more than 1 hour, and children requiring care above the level of comfort of the local hospital
claims.source_text:
Respiratory or haemodynamic compromise
  - Prolonged febrile seizure
  - Persistent altered mental status (>1 hour)
  - Children requiring care above the level of comfort of the local hospital

claims.claim: Discharge should be considered when the child has returned to normal neurological state following a simple febrile seizure and the underlying illness has been assessed and managed appropriately
claims.source_text:
Returned to normal neurological state following simple febrile seizure
  - Underlying illness has been assessed and managed appropriately

claims.claim: All families should receive education prior to discharge including seizure first aid and a febrile seizure handout, and if the seizure lasted more than 5 minutes clinicians should consider providing an emergency medication management plan and parent midazolam training
claims.source_text:
All families should receive education prior to discharge which includes:
    - Seizure first aid
    - Febrile seizure handout
    - If seizure >5 minutes, consider providing emergency medication management plan and parent midazolam training

claims.claim: Follow-up should be arranged if required for the underlying illness and outpatient paediatric follow-up should be considered
claims.source_text:
Arrange follow-up if required for the underlying illness
  - Consider outpatient paediatric follow-up, see below

claims.claim: Outpatient follow-up should be considered when risk factors are present for development of epilepsy, being prolonged febrile seizure, family history of epilepsy, neurocutaneous stigmata identified on examination, recurrent complex febrile seizures, and developmental impairment
claims.source_text:
Risk factors are present for development of epilepsy
    - Prolonged febrile seizure
    - Family history of epilepsy
    - Neurocutaneous stigmata identified on examination
    - Recurrent complex febrile seizures
    - Developmental impairment

claims.claim: Further investigations may include EEG, neuroimaging and genetic testing, and genetic testing may be recommended in higher risk groups being prolonged febrile convulsions in a child under 18 months, febrile seizures in children over 6 years, and associated developmental impairment
claims.source_text:
Further investigations may include EEG, neuroimaging and genetic testing
  - Genetic testing may be recommended in higher risk groups
    - Prolonged febrile convulsions in child <18 months
    - Febrile seizures in children >6 years
    - Associated developmental impairment

claims.claim: The guideline was last updated February 2026 and is PIC endorsed
claims.source_text: Last updated February 2026 … PIC Endorsed

claims.claim: The guideline links parent information sheets from Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland and Western Australia, including a Western Australian resource titled Febrile convulsions - Keeping our Mob Healthy
claims.source_text: Febrile seizures (Vic) … Febrile convulsion (NSW) … Febrile convulsions (QLD) … Febrile-convulsions---Keeping-our-Mob-Healthy.pdf
